67076.e: The Spanish brought the Catholic days of remembering the dead to Mexico. They mixed with old customs of the Aztecs and other peoples.
67076.m: The Day of the Dead falls on All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.

67077.q: Which ancient people of Mexico already had customs for the dead that live on in the Day of the Dead?
67077.e: The Aztecs honoured their dead with festivals. Their customs later mixed with the Catholic holidays of the Spanish.
67077.m: The Day of the Dead combines Aztec and Christian customs.

67078.q: Which organisation added the Day of the Dead to its list of intangible cultural heritage?
67078.e: UNESCO protects not only buildings but also living customs. The Mexican celebration of the dead has been on this list since 2008.
67078.m: The Day of the Dead is part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.

67079.q: Which larger group of peoples do the Lakota belong to?
67079.e: The Lakota are the westernmost group of the Sioux. They lived as bison hunters on the Great Plains of North America.
67079.m: The Lakota belong to the Sioux.

67080.q: In which season do the Lakota hold the Sun Dance?
67080.e: The Sun Dance takes place in early summer or summer, usually around the time of the longest days. Many families gather then.
67080.m: The Sun Dance is held in summer.

67081.q: Which tree stands as the sacred centre of the dance ground at the Sun Dance?
67081.e: A cottonwood tree, a kind of poplar, is solemnly cut down and set up in the middle. The dancers dance around this tree.
67081.m: At the Sun Dance, a cottonwood tree stands in the middle.

67082.q: Where do the Lakota cleanse themselves with hot steam before the Sun Dance?
a: On the shore of a lake
67082.e: In the sweat lodge, water is poured over hot stones. The steam and the prayers are meant to cleanse body and mind.
67082.m: Before the Sun Dance, the Lakota cleanse themselves in the sweat lodge.

67083.q: According to Lakota tradition, which sacred female figure brought the sacred pipe?
67083.e: According to tradition, she taught the Lakota important rituals. That is why the birth of a white bison calf is still seen as a special sign today.
67083.m: White Buffalo Calf Woman brought the sacred pipe to the Lakota.

67084.q: Which animal was most important to the Lakota for life and in their beliefs?
67084.e: The bison provided meat, hides, tools and material for tents. It was seen as a gift and was treated with respect.
67084.m: The bison was the most important animal for the Lakota.

67085.q: Which mountain range in South Dakota is sacred to the Lakota?
67085.e: The Lakota call the Black Hills Paha Sapa. Today the Mount Rushmore monument is also there, which many Lakota feel is an insult.
67085.m: The Black Hills are sacred to the Lakota.

67086.q: What do the dancers usually go without for days during the Sun Dance?
67086.e: The dancers fast during the ceremony, which usually lasts four days. They make this sacrifice for the good of their community.
67086.m: The dancers fast during the Sun Dance.

67087.q: From 1883, what was the situation for a long time in the USA for the Lakota Sun Dance?
a: It was compulsory in all schools
67087.e: From 1883 the Sun Dance was banned in the USA. Only a law from 1978 explicitly protected such ceremonies.
67087.m: The Sun Dance was banned in the USA for a long time.

67088.q: According to Inuit belief, where does the sea goddess Sedna live?
a: At the bottom of the sea
67088.e: From the bottom of the sea, Sedna rules over the sea animals. When she is angry, she holds the animals back and the hunters find nothing to catch.
67088.m: Sedna is the sea goddess of the Inuit.

67089.q: According to the Inuit myth, what came from the sea goddess’s fingers?
67089.e: According to the legend, the woman’s fingers were cut off as she fell into the sea. The finger joints became seals, walruses and whales.
67089.m: The sea goddess’s fingers became seals and whales.

67090.q: What is a shaman called among the Inuit?
67090.e: According to the belief, the angakkuq could travel to the spirits. He or she was meant to heal the sick and put right broken taboos.
67090.m: Among the Inuit, a shaman is called an angakkuq.

67091.q: According to some Inuit stories, what are the northern lights?
67091.e: In many areas people believed that the dead played ball in the sky. The dancing lights in the night sky showed this game.
67091.m: For some Inuit, the northern lights are souls at play.

67092.q: What does “Sila” stand for in Inuit belief?
67092.e: Sila stands for air, weather and the order of the world. The word also means mind or reason.
67092.m: For the Inuit, Sila is the spirit of air and weather.

67093.q: Why did Inuit hunters often give a seal they had killed a sip of fresh water?
67093.e: Seals live in salt water and, according to the belief, are thirsty. Whoever honoured their soul like this could hope for more luck in hunting.
67093.m: The Inuit honoured the soul of a hunted seal with fresh water.

67094.q: In the traditions of Greenland, what is a tupilaq?
67094.e: According to the belief, a tupilaq was made from bones and skin to harm an enemy. Today artists carve small tupilaq figures from bone or stone.
67094.m: A tupilaq is a magical figure from Greenland.

67095.q: How did the explorer Knud Rasmussen travel through the Arctic to collect Inuit stories?
67095.e: From 1921 to 1924, Knud Rasmussen travelled by dog sledge from Greenland to Alaska. He wrote down many Inuit stories and songs.
67095.m: Knud Rasmussen collected many Inuit myths.

67096.q: Which religion did missionaries bring to Greenland in the 18th century?
67096.e: The Norwegian pastor Hans Egede came to Greenland in 1721. After that, Christianity spread there.

67097.q: Who is Pachamama in the belief of the Andean peoples?
67097.e: Pachamama gives fertility and good harvests. Many people in the Andes still honour her today.
67097.m: Pachamama is the Mother Earth of the Andean peoples.

67098.q: What does the Quechua word “pacha” in the name Pachamama mean?
67098.e: The word “pacha” means world, earth and time all at once. “Mama” means mother.
67098.m: In Quechua, pacha means world, earth and time.

67099.q: In which month is Pachamama especially celebrated in the Andes?
67099.e: In the Andes, August is seen as the month of Pachamama. According to the belief, the earth is hungry then and waits for gifts before sowing.
67099.m: Pachamama is especially celebrated in August.

67100.q: How are offerings for Pachamama often made?
a: They are put into a hole in the ground
They are thrown into the sea
They are burned in the temple
67100.e: Families dig a hole and fill it with food, drinks and coca. In this way the earth is meant to be “fed”.
67100.m: Gifts for Pachamama are put into the earth.

67101.q: What is the drink chicha, which is given to Pachamama as a gift, made from?
67101.e: Chicha is a maize beer from the Andes. Before drinking, many people pour a few drops on the ground, giving Mother Earth the first sip.
67101.m: Pachamama is often given maize beer called chicha.

67102.q: What did Ecuador give nature in its constitution in 2008?
67102.e: Ecuador’s constitution also calls nature Pacha Mama. There it receives its own rights, which can be enforced in court.
67102.m: In 2008 Ecuador gave nature its own rights.

67103.q: How does a law in Bolivia describe Mother Earth?
a: As a living system with its own rights
As a store of raw materials for companies
As the home of the dead
67103.e: The law from 2010 is based on the ideas of the Andean peoples. It describes the earth as a living system with its own rights.
67103.m: In Bolivia, Mother Earth has its own rights.

67104.q: According to the belief of the Andean peoples, where do the mountain spirits, the apus, live?
a: At the bottom of the sea
In the clouds over the desert
67104.e: According to the belief, the apus live in the high peaks. They protect the people, animals and fields around them.
67104.m: The mountain spirits of the Andes live in the peaks.

67105.q: Around which lake do the Aymara, who honour Pachamama, live?
67105.e: The Aymara live mainly around Lake Titicaca in Bolivia and Peru. For them too, Pachamama is a central figure.
67105.m: The Aymara live around Lake Titicaca.

67106.q: Which basic right in the Federal Constitution also protects people who do not believe in God?
67106.e: Freedom of religion and conscience allows every person to have a religion or none. Nobody may be forced into it.
67106.m: In Switzerland everyone may believe or not believe.

67107.q: What is belief in one or more gods, the opposite of atheism, called?
67107.e: Theism is belief in God or gods. Atheism rejects this belief.
67107.m: Theists believe in God, atheists do not.

67110.q: How do many atheists explain how the world and life began?
a: Through natural processes such as the Big Bang and evolution
Not at all, they are not interested
67110.e: Atheists do not believe that a god created the world. They explain it through the natural sciences.
67110.m: Atheists explain the world without God.

67112.q: What is an “atheist” according to their own conviction?
a: Someone who does not believe that God exists.
Someone who believes in many gods.
Someone who believes in God but not in the Church.
67112.e: Atheists are convinced that there is no God, or they have no belief in God. That is different from criticising the Church.
67112.m: Atheists have no belief in God.

67113.q: What does an agnostic say about the question of whether God exists?
67113.e: Agnostics think the question about God cannot be answered. They commit neither to belief nor to unbelief.
67113.m: Agnostics say that nothing certain can be known about God.

67114.q: What does the Greek word “ágnostos”, from which “agnosticism” comes, mean?
67114.e: “Gnosis” means knowledge, “a-” means “not”. So agnostos means “not knowable” or “unknown”.
67114.m: The word agnosticism contains the Greek word for knowledge.

67115.q: What is the difference between an atheist and an agnostic?
a: The atheist does not believe in God, the agnostic says you cannot know
The agnostic does not believe in God, the atheist says you cannot know
67115.e: Atheists have no belief in God. Agnostics leave the question open because, in their view, nothing certain can be known about it.
67115.m: Agnostics leave the question of God open.

67116.q: Thomas Huxley invented the word “agnostic”. Which theory did he defend especially fiercely?
67116.e: Huxley stood up for Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution so strongly that he was called “Darwin’s bulldog”.
67116.m: Huxley defended Darwin’s theory of evolution.

67117.q: Which famous naturalist called himself an agnostic in his autobiography?
67117.e: Charles Darwin wrote that the word “agnostic” described his view best. When he was young, he had been intended to become a clergyman.
67117.m: Charles Darwin saw himself as an agnostic.

67118.q: What does the prefix “a-” mean in the words agnostic and atheist?
67118.e: The Greek prefix “a-” makes a word negative. So atheist means “without God” and agnostic “not knowing”.

67119.q: What do you call people who do not belong to any religious community?
67119.e: Non-denominational people do not belong to any church or religious community. In Switzerland this is now about a third of the population.
67119.m: Someone who does not belong to a religious community is non-denominational.

67120.q: What is at the centre of humanism?
a: The human being and their dignity
67120.e: The word comes from the Latin “humanus”, meaning human. Humanists put the human being, their education and their dignity at the centre.
67120.m: In humanism, the human being is at the centre.

67121.q: In which period did humanism begin as an educational movement?
67121.e: Renaissance humanism began in Italy in the 14th century. Scholars rediscovered the texts of the ancient Greeks and Romans.

67122.q: Which motto of the humanists means “to the sources”?
67122.e: With “ad fontes”, the humanists demanded that people read the original ancient texts rather than only later interpretations.
67122.m: The humanists wanted to go back to the sources.

67123.q: Which famous humanist lived in Basel for a long time and is buried in Basel Minster?
67123.e: Erasmus of Rotterdam worked with printers in Basel for many years. He died in Basel in 1536.
67123.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam is buried in Basel Minster.

67124.q: Which important work did Erasmus of Rotterdam publish in Basel in 1516?
67124.e: In 1516 the New Testament in the original Greek text with a Latin translation was published by Johannes Froben in Basel. Martin Luther later used it for his translation of the Bible.
67124.m: Erasmus made the Greek New Testament known from Basel.

67125.q: What does today’s secular humanism base its ethics on?
67125.e: Secular humanists base values not on religion but on reason, science and compassion. Human dignity is the most important measure for them.
67125.m: Secular humanism grounds morality without God.

67126.q: Which subjects are traditionally at the centre of a “humanist grammar school”?
67126.e: Humanist grammar schools focus on the old languages of antiquity, because the humanists wanted to read the ancient texts in the original.
67126.m: At a humanist grammar school you learn Latin and Greek.

67127.q: Which Zurich reformer was strongly influenced by the humanism of Erasmus when he was young?
67127.e: Huldrych Zwingli read Erasmus’s writings with enthusiasm and visited him in Basel in 1516. The humanist demand to read the Bible in the original language shaped his Reformation in Zurich.
67127.m: Zwingli was a humanist before he became a reformer.

67128.q: What is typical of a secular state?
a: It is independent of religious institutions.
It tells everyone which religion to follow.
67128.e: A secular state does not base its laws on a religion and does not favour any faith community. Religions may still be practised freely.
67128.m: A secular state is religiously neutral.

67129.q: What do you call a state in which religious leaders hold political power?
67129.e: In a theocracy, rule is justified by religion and carried out by clergy. “Theos” means god, “kratos” rule.
67129.m: In a theocracy, religious leaders rule.

67130.q: Since the separation of Church and state in France, what has the state stopped paying for almost everywhere?
67130.e: The law of 1905 separating Church and state is the basis of French “laïcité”. Since then the state has paid no priests almost anywhere; one exception is Alsace with parts of Lorraine.
67130.m: France separated Church and state in 1905.

67131.q: In which country is the Anglican Church the state church, with the king as its secular head?
67131.e: The Church of England is the established church in England. The British monarch is its “Supreme Governor”, its secular head.
67131.m: In England the king is head of the state church.

67132.q: What is the French word for the strict separation of state and religion?
67132.e: “Laïcité” refers to the religious neutrality of the French state. In English it is sometimes called laicism or secularism.
67132.m: The French call the separation of state and religion “laïcité”.

67133.q: Why is there usually no cross hanging in classrooms of state schools in Switzerland?
a: The school must be religiously neutral.
The teachers do not want one.
67133.e: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court decided that a crucifix in a classroom of a state school breaks religious neutrality. The school must treat all children equally, whatever their religion.
67133.m: State schools in Switzerland must be religiously neutral.

67134.q: What is meant by the “secularisation” of a society?
67134.e: Secularisation is the process in which religion becomes less important in public and private life. The Latin “saeculum” means age or world.
67134.m: In secularisation, religion becomes less important.

67135.q: The Aargau monastery dispute of 1841 made the quarrel between the cantons worse. Which war did this quarrel lead to in 1847?
67135.e: In 1841 the canton of Aargau closed its monasteries, including Muri Abbey. This outraged the Catholic cantons. The tensions led in 1847 to the Sonderbund War, Switzerland’s last civil war.
67135.m: The monastery dispute in Aargau was a step towards the Sonderbund War.

67136.q: Which freedom does Article 15 of the Swiss Federal Constitution protect?
67136.e: Article 15 of the Federal Constitution protects the right to choose your religion freely and to practise it alone or with others.
67136.m: The Federal Constitution protects freedom of religion.

67137.q: What applied to the Jesuit order in Switzerland from 1848 to 1973?
67137.e: After the Sonderbund War, the Federal Constitution banned the Jesuit order. The voters lifted this ban in 1973.
67137.m: The ban on Jesuits applied in Switzerland until 1973.

67138.q: According to the Federal Constitution, who is responsible for the relationship between Church and state?
67138.e: Article 72 of the Federal Constitution gives the cantons the job of regulating the relationship between Church and state. That is why there are 26 different solutions.
67138.m: In Switzerland, the cantons regulate Church and state.

67139.q: What did Swiss voters add to the Federal Constitution in November 2009?
67139.e: On 29 November 2009 the minaret initiative was accepted with about 57.5 per cent voting yes. Since then Article 72 has banned the building of new minarets.
67139.m: Since 2009 the Federal Constitution has banned the building of minarets.

67140.q: With which words does the preamble of the Swiss Federal Constitution begin?
a: In the name of Almighty God!
One for all, all for one!
67140.e: Like the earlier ones, the Federal Constitution of 1999 begins by calling on God. Even so, the Confederation is religiously neutral.
67140.m: The Federal Constitution begins by calling on God.

67141.q: Which group in Switzerland only received the right to live wherever they chose in 1866?
67141.e: The Federal Constitution of 1848 granted freedom of residence only to Christians. Only in 1866 did Swiss Jews also receive this right.
67141.m: Jews only received freedom of residence in 1866.

67142.q: What does the freedom of religion and conscience in the Federal Constitution also expressly guarantee?
a: Nobody has to belong to a religion.
You may never change your religion.
67142.e: According to the Federal Constitution, nobody may be forced to join a religious community or take part in a religious act. This negative freedom of religion also protects non-denominational people.
67142.m: Freedom of religion also protects the right not to belong to any religion.

67143.q: What did the bishopric article, which voters removed from the Federal Constitution in 2001, require?
a: New dioceses needed permission from the Confederation
Every municipality had to build a church
Priests were elected by the Federal Council
67143.e: The bishopric article of 1874 required that new dioceses could only be set up with the approval of the Confederation. It was the last special religious rule in the Federal Constitution.
67143.m: Since 2001 a new diocese no longer needs the approval of the Confederation.

67144.q: According to the Federal Statistical Office, which group was the largest in Switzerland in 2023?
67144.e: In 2023 about 36 per cent of the population aged 15 and over had no religious affiliation. So, as in 2022, they were ahead of the Roman Catholics.
67144.m: People with no religious affiliation are now the largest group in Switzerland.

67145.q: Roughly what percentage of the population was Roman Catholic in 2023?
67145.e: According to the structural survey of the Federal Statistical Office, about 31 per cent were Roman Catholic in 2023. Their share has been falling for decades.
67145.m: About a third of the population is Roman Catholic.

67146.q: Roughly what percentage of the population was Protestant Reformed in 2023?
67146.e: In 2023 about 19 per cent of the population aged 15 and over belonged to the Protestant Reformed Church. In 1970 it was still almost half.
67146.m: About one person in five in Switzerland is Reformed.

67147.q: Which non-Christian religion is the largest in Switzerland (as of 2023)?
67147.e: About 6 per cent of the population belong to a Muslim community. Many Muslims have roots in the Balkans or in Turkey.
67147.m: Islam is the largest non-Christian religion in Switzerland.

67148.q: Which federal office collects the figures on religious affiliation in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
67148.e: Every year the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) asks about 200,000 people in its structural survey. The shares of the religions are calculated from this.
67148.m: The religion statistics come from the Federal Statistical Office.

67150.q: How many people does the Federal Statistical Office ask today for the religion figures?
67150.e: Until 2000 all residents were asked every ten years. Since 2010 the FSO has used registers and yearly samples such as the structural survey.
67150.m: Today there is a sample survey every year instead of the census.

67151.q: Which two Christian denominations have shaped Switzerland most strongly since the Reformation?
67151.e: From the 16th century the cantons were either Catholic or Reformed. This split shaped Swiss history until the 20th century.
67151.m: For a long time Switzerland was shaped by Catholics and Reformed Protestants.

67152.q: What is a “Landeskirche” (recognised national church) in Switzerland?
a: A church officially recognised by the canton under public law
A church only in the countryside
A church paid for by the Confederation
67152.e: Landeskirchen are recognised by a canton under public law. This gives them a special link with the state, but they remain independent.
67152.m: Landeskirchen are churches recognised by the canton.

67153.q: Which three Christian churches are recognised as Landeskirchen in many cantons?
a: Roman Catholic, Protestant Reformed, Christ Catholic
67153.e: In most cantons the Roman Catholic and the Protestant Reformed churches are recognised, and in many also the small Christ Catholic Church.
67153.m: Most cantons recognise three Christian Landeskirchen.

67154.q: What right do recognised Landeskirchen have in most cantons?
67154.e: The cantons allow the recognised churches to collect church taxes from their members. In many cantons companies pay church taxes too.

67155.q: Why did the Christ Catholic Church come about in the 19th century?
a: In protest against the infallibility of the Pope
Because of a quarrel about building a church
67155.e: In 1870 the First Vatican Council declared the Pope infallible in matters of faith. Catholics who rejected this founded the Christ Catholic Church in Switzerland.
67155.m: The Christ Catholic Church rejects the infallibility of the Pope.

67156.q: Which non-Christian community is officially recognised in several cantons, such as Zurich and Basel-Stadt?
67156.e: Several cantons, including Basel-Stadt, Bern and Zurich, have recognised Jewish communities under public law.
67156.m: In some cantons Jewish communities are also recognised.

67157.q: What do the Landeskirchen use their church taxes for, among other things?
67157.e: With the taxes the churches pay for clergy, services, youth work and help for people in need. Since 2020 the Reformed churches have been joined together in the Protestant Church of Switzerland.
67157.m: Church taxes pay for pastoral care and social work.

67158.q: In many Reformed parishes in Switzerland, who elects the minister?
67158.e: Reformed parishes are organised democratically. The members who have a vote elect their ministers and decide on the budget.
67158.m: In Reformed parishes the members elect their minister.

67160.q: Roughly what share of people in Switzerland had no religious affiliation around 1970?
67160.e: Around 1970 only about 1 per cent of the population had no religious affiliation. By 2022 the share had risen to about a third.
67160.m: Fifty years ago almost everyone in Switzerland belonged to a church.

67161.q: In which canton do more than half of the people have no religious affiliation?
67161.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, in 2022 about 56 per cent in Basel-Stadt had no religious affiliation, and about 53 per cent in Neuchâtel. In rural Catholic cantons the share is much smaller.
67161.m: In Basel-Stadt most people have no religious affiliation.

67162.q: Why are there only a few people with no religious affiliation in Appenzell Innerrhoden?
a: Leaving the church is forbidden there
67162.e: In 2022 only about 15 per cent in Appenzell Innerrhoden had no religious affiliation. The rural canton is strongly Catholic.
67162.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden has the fewest people with no religious affiliation.

67163.q: Who is more likely to have no religious affiliation in Switzerland?
67163.e: Among 25 to 34-year-olds, about 42 per cent had no religious affiliation in 2022. Among the over-75s it was only about 16 per cent.
67163.m: Younger adults more often have no religious affiliation than older people.

67164.q: Where in Switzerland is the share of people with no religious affiliation higher?
67164.e: In 2022 about 36 per cent in urban areas had no religious affiliation, and about 28 per cent in the countryside.
67164.m: There are more people with no religious affiliation in towns than in the countryside.

67165.q: In which city is the “House of Religions, Dialogue of Cultures”?
67165.e: The House of Religions is in the west of Bern, in the Ausserholligen district. It is known all over Switzerland for dialogue between religions.
67165.m: The House of Religions is in Bern.

67166.q: What does the House of Religions in Bern want to be a place for?
67166.e: The House of Religions opened in 2014. People of different religions and cultures are meant to meet and exchange ideas there.
67166.m: The House of Religions encourages meeting and dialogue.

67167.q: Who may visit the House of Religions in Bern?
67167.e: The House of Religions is open to everyone. There are guided tours, a restaurant and events.
67167.m: The House of Religions is open to everyone.

67168.q: What is special about the House of Religions in Bern?
a: Several religions have their prayer rooms under one roof.
It is the oldest church in Switzerland.
It is a museum with no visitors.
The Bishop of Basel lives there.
67168.e: Under one roof there are, for example, a Hindu temple, a mosque, a church and Buddhist and Alevi rooms. The house encourages meeting and dialogue.
67168.m: In the House of Religions, different religions pray under one roof.

67169.q: Which religion has its own temple in the House of Religions in Bern?
a: The religion of the ancient Egyptians
67169.e: The House of Religions includes a Hindu temple, a mosque and a church, among others.
67169.m: There is a Hindu temple in the House of Religions in Bern.

67170.q: What has been special about the Hindu community in the House of Religions since 2015?
a: Women are also ordained as priests.
The temple is only open at night.
There are no statues of gods.
67170.e: Since 2015 the Hindu community in Bern has ordained women as priests. In the countries the community comes from, this is hardly possible.
67170.m: The Hindu temple in Bern also has women priests.

67171.q: How many religions have prayer rooms in the House of Religions in Bern?
67171.e: Under one roof there are a Hindu temple, a mosque, a church and Buddhist and Alevi rooms.
67171.m: In the House of Religions, several religions pray under one roof.

67172.q: What is the aim of interfaith dialogue?
a: That religions understand each other and live together peacefully
That everyone takes on the same religion
67172.e: In interfaith dialogue, members of different religions learn from each other and overcome prejudices. Nobody has to give up their faith.
67172.m: Interfaith dialogue encourages understanding and peace.

67173.q: What is the cooperation between the different Christian churches called?
67173.e: Ecumenism means the conversation and cooperation between Christian denominations. Dialogue between different religions, on the other hand, is called interfaith.
67173.m: Ecumenism is the dialogue between Christian churches.

67174.q: What can you do, for example, during the “Week of Religions” in Switzerland?
a: Only go to your own church
67174.e: Every year at the beginning of November, many religious communities open their doors. You can visit places of worship and ask questions.
67174.m: During the Week of Religions you get to know other religions.

67175.q: Which attitude helps when talking with people of another religion?
a: Convincing the other person at all costs
Talking only about your own religion
67175.e: Interfaith dialogue is about understanding each other. Whoever listens and asks questions breaks down prejudices.
67175.m: In dialogue between religions, people listen to each other.

67176.q: Which three religions all trace themselves back to Abraham?
67176.e: Judaism, Christianity and Islam see Abraham as the father of their faith. That is why they often hold talks with each other, for example in the Swiss Council of Religions.
67176.m: Judaism, Christianity and Islam trace themselves back to Abraham.

67177.q: Which rule do almost all religions know?
a: Treat others as you want to be treated
Do not eat meat on Fridays
67177.e: This Golden Rule is found in many religions. The Swiss theologian Hans Küng saw it as a value shared by all religions.
67177.m: Almost all religions know the Golden Rule.

67179.q: What did representatives of many religions do in Assisi in 1986 at the Pope’s invitation?
67179.e: In 1986 Pope John Paul II invited representatives of many religions to Assisi, the town of St Francis. Together they prayed for peace.
67179.m: In 1986 representatives of many religions prayed for peace in Assisi.

67180.q: What does the abbreviation ERG stand for in the Swiss curriculum Lehrplan 21?
67180.e: ERG stands for Ethik, Religionen, Gemeinschaft, meaning ethics, religions, community. In this area you learn about values, religions and living together.
67180.m: ERG stands for ethics, religions, community.

67181.q: In primary school, which subject area does ERG belong to in Lehrplan 21?
67181.e: In cycles 1 and 2, ERG is part of the subject area “Nature, Humans, Society” (NMG). In lower secondary school, ERG is taught as a separate area.
67181.m: In primary school, ERG belongs to Nature, Humans, Society.

67182.q: How is ERG taught at state schools?
a: Independently of any faith and neutrally
67182.e: The lessons give information about different religions and world views without promoting any one of them. All children can take part.
67182.m: ERG gives neutral information about religions.

67183.q: In Switzerland, who usually gives denominational religious education, for example before confirmation?
67183.e: Denominational lessons are the responsibility of the churches, for example confirmation classes in the Catholic parish or in the Reformed church.
67183.m: The churches are responsible for denominational religious education.

67184.q: What is the subject on religions and ethics called at secondary level in the canton of Zurich?
67184.e: In the canton of Zurich, the compulsory subject is called “Religions, Cultures, Ethics” (RKE). It is neutral with regard to denomination.
67184.m: Zurich calls the subject Religions, Cultures, Ethics.

67185.q: For how many cantons was Lehrplan 21 developed?
67185.e: Lehrplan 21 applies to the 21 German-speaking and multilingual cantons. That is where its name comes from.
67185.m: Lehrplan 21 is called that because it applies to 21 cantons.

67186.q: Which skill should you especially practise in the subject ERG?
67186.e: ERG encourages you to think about values and to treat people with other beliefs with respect. This includes weighing up arguments.
67186.m: In ERG you learn to respect other beliefs.

67187.q: What are rules and values that a community shares for living together called?
67187.e: Norms are rules for behaviour, for example laws or rules of good manners. They are based on values such as fairness or honesty.
67187.m: Norms regulate how people live together in a community.

a: What good and right action is
67188.e: Ethics is a part of philosophy. It asks how people should act and how moral judgements can be justified.
67188.m: Ethics asks what good and right action is.

67189.q: What is a good character trait such as courage, honesty or fairness called?
67189.e: Virtues are lasting good qualities of a person. Even the ancient philosophers named justice, courage, moderation and wisdom as the cardinal virtues.

67190.q: What do you call a situation in which you have to choose between two bad options?
67190.e: In a dilemma there is no solution without a disadvantage. In ethics, dilemmas help you think about values.
67190.m: A dilemma is a difficult situation with no easy solution.

67191.e: Immanuel Kant said you should only act according to a rule that you could want to apply to everyone.
67191.m: The categorical imperative comes from Immanuel Kant.

67192.q: What is the inner voice that tells you whether an action is good or bad called?
67192.e: Conscience is the inner awareness of good and evil. With freedom of conscience, the Federal Constitution also protects personal moral beliefs.
67192.m: Our conscience helps us tell good from evil.

a: The rules and values by which people act
67193.e: Morals are the actual values and rules of a group. Ethics thinks about them and checks whether they are well founded.
67193.m: Morals are values that people live by; ethics thinks about them.

67196.q: Which story does the Islamic Festival of Sacrifice remember?
a: Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice his son
67196.e: The Festival of Sacrifice, in Arabic “Eid al-Adha”, remembers Abraham (Ibrahim), who wanted to obey God. God had an animal sacrificed instead of the son.
67196.m: The Festival of Sacrifice remembers Abraham.

67197.q: Which New Year festival do Baha'is, Kurds and people from Iran celebrate at the start of spring?
67197.e: Nowruz means “new day” and is celebrated around 21 March. For Baha'is it is also a religious holiday.
67197.m: Nowruz is the New Year festival at the start of spring.

67198.q: Which Jewish holiday is the Day of Atonement and is marked by fasting?
67198.e: Yom Kippur is the holiest Jewish holiday. Believers fast for about 25 hours and ask for forgiveness.
67198.m: Yom Kippur is the Jewish Day of Atonement.

67199.q: Which event does the Christian festival of Pentecost remember?
a: The sending of the Holy Spirit
67199.e: Pentecost is celebrated 50 days after Easter. According to the Bible, the Holy Spirit came down on the disciples. In most cantons there is no school on Whit Monday.
67199.m: At Pentecost, Christians celebrate the sending of the Holy Spirit.

67200.q: What can parents in Switzerland usually apply for on behalf of their child on major religious holidays?
67200.e: In many cantons, pupils may be excused from lessons on major holidays of their religion if they apply. The exact rules are set by the cantons.
67200.m: On major religious holidays you can be excused from lessons.

67201.q: On which Sunday is the Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer?
a: On the third Sunday in September
On the first Sunday in May
On the last Sunday in June
On the second Sunday in December
67201.e: In most cantons this day of prayer is held on the third Sunday in September. Instead, Geneva celebrates the “Jeûne genevois” in September.
67201.m: The Federal Day of Prayer is on the third Sunday in September.

67202.q: Why is Ascension Day always on a Thursday?
a: It is 40 days after Easter, counting Easter itself.
67202.e: Ascension is celebrated on the 40th day of the Easter season, with Easter Sunday counted as the first day. Counting from a Sunday, you always land on a Thursday.
67202.m: Ascension Day always falls on a Thursday.

67203.q: Which Catholic holiday is a school holiday only in mainly Catholic cantons, for example Lucerne?
67203.e: Corpus Christi is celebrated with processions on the second Thursday after Pentecost. It is a school holiday mainly in Catholic cantons.
67203.m: Corpus Christi is a holiday mainly in Catholic cantons.

67204.q: On which continent was Augustine born?
67204.e: Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste in North Africa, in today's Algeria. At that time the area belonged to the Roman Empire.

67205.q: What does Augustine describe in his famous book ‘Confessions’?
a: His own life and his path to faith
The history of the Roman Empire
The animals and plants of Africa
Rules for life in a monastery
67205.e: In the ‘Confessions’ (Latin Confessiones), Augustine tells openly about his life and his conversion. The work is regarded as one of the first autobiographies.
67205.m: In the ‘Confessions’ Augustine tells the story of his life.

67206.q: In which North African city was Augustine bishop for more than 30 years?
67206.e: Augustine became Bishop of Hippo Regius in 395. That is why he is also called Augustine of Hippo.

67207.q: According to tradition, who prayed for many years that Augustine would become a Christian?
67207.e: His mother Monica was a Christian and prayed for her son for many years. Today she is honoured as a saint.
67207.m: Augustine's mother prayed for him for a long time.

67208.q: What are important early teachers of the Church such as Augustine called?
67208.e: Church Fathers are important Christian writers of the first centuries. Augustine is one of the best known; he wrote, for example, ‘The City of God’.

67209.q: What is it called when someone like Augustine consciously turns to the Christian faith as an adult?
67209.e: Augustine only found the Christian faith when he was over 30. In 387 he was baptised in Milan by Bishop Ambrose.
67209.m: Augustine converted to Christianity as an adult.

67210.q: Before his conversion Augustine was a teacher of rhetoric. What is rhetoric?
67210.e: Rhetoric is the art of public speaking. Augustine was so good at it that he got a respected post in Milan.
67210.m: Augustine was first a teacher of public speaking.

67211.q: Which office did Augustine take on in North Africa a few years after his baptism?
67211.e: Augustine returned to North Africa and became Bishop of Hippo in 395. He held this office for more than 30 years.
67211.m: Augustine became a bishop in North Africa.

67212.q: Which order, to which Martin Luther later also belonged, follows a rule of Augustine?
67212.e: The Augustinians live by the Rule of Augustine. In 1505 Martin Luther entered a monastery of the Augustinian Hermits in Erfurt.
67212.m: The Augustinian order is named after Augustine.

67213.q: What happened in 1944, during the Second World War, to the monastery of Monte Cassino founded by Benedict?
a: It was moved into the sea
67213.e: During the fighting around Monte Cassino, the Allies bombed the monastery in February 1944. It was rebuilt after the war.
67213.m: Monte Cassino was destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt.

67214.q: Why are the Benedictines also called ‘black monks’?
a: Because they only pray at night
Because they only eat black bread
67214.e: Benedictines traditionally wear a black habit. This sets them apart from, for example, the Cistercians, who wear white.

67215.q: Which special vow binds Benedictines to their monastery for life?
67215.e: Benedictines promise ‘stabilitas loci’, stability of place. They remain part of the same monastic community all their lives.
67215.m: Benedictines promise to stay in their monastery.

67216.q: Benedict has been patron saint of which continent since 1964?
67216.e: Pope Paul VI declared Benedict patron of Europe in 1964. His monasteries shaped European culture for centuries.
67216.m: Benedict is the patron saint of Europe.

67217.q: According to tradition, which of Benedict's relatives also lived a monastic life?
67217.e: According to tradition, Scholastica was Benedict's twin sister. She led a community of nuns near Monte Cassino.
67217.m: Benedict's twin sister also lived in a convent.

67218.q: Which pope chose the name Benedict in 2005?
67218.e: Joseph Ratzinger took the name Benedict XVI as pope. In this way he also recalled Saint Benedict, the patron saint of Europe.
67218.m: Pope Benedict XVI chose the name of Saint Benedict.

67219.q: What is the head of a Benedictine monastery called?
67219.e: According to the Rule of Benedict, an abbot leads the monastery like a father. The word comes from the Aramaic ‘abba’, meaning father.
67219.m: An abbot leads a Benedictine monastery.

67220.q: How did Benedict live as a young man before he founded monasteries?
a: As a hermit in a cave
As a soldier in the army
67220.e: Benedict withdrew to a cave near Subiaco, east of Rome. Soon followers gathered around him there.
67220.m: Benedict first lived as a hermit.

67221.q: In which country did Benedict of Nursia live about 1500 years ago?
67221.e: Benedict came from Nursia, today Norcia in central Italy. He founded the monastery of Monte Cassino between Rome and Naples.

67222.q: Hildegard of Bingen was her parents' child number what?
67222.e: Hildegard was the tenth child of a noble family. Her parents dedicated her to God, like a ‘tithe’ of their children.
67222.m: Hildegard was her parents' tenth child.

67223.q: What is the head of a convent, as Hildegard was, called?
67223.e: Hildegard became the leader of her community of women. The head of a convent is called an abbess; for a monastery of men it is an abbot.

67224.q: What are women who, like Hildegard, live in a convent by a religious rule called?
67224.e: Hildegard first lived for many years in the monastery on the Disibodenberg. Women who live in a convent by a religious rule are called nuns or sisters.
67224.m: Women in a convent are called nuns.

67225.q: Which grain did Hildegard praise as especially healthy?
67225.e: Hildegard praised spelt as especially easy to digest. Maize only came to Europe after the discovery of America.

67226.q: What did Hildegard mainly treat sick people with?
67226.e: In her books, such as ‘Causae et curae’, Hildegard described many medicinal plants. There were no modern medicines in the Middle Ages.

67227.q: What did Hildegard do that was very unusual for a nun of her time?
a: She preached in public on her travels
67227.e: Hildegard went on preaching tours, including to Mainz, Bamberg, Trier and Cologne. For a woman of her time, preaching in public to ordinary people was extraordinary.
67227.m: Hildegard travelled the country as a preacher.

67228.q: How did Hildegard communicate with popes, emperors and other important people?
67228.e: Hundreds of Hildegard's letters have survived. She wrote to Bernard of Clairvaux, to popes and to Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, among others.
67228.m: Hildegard wrote many letters to important people.

67229.q: What did Hildegard call the life force that makes everything in nature grow and flower?
67229.e: Hildegard spoke of ‘viriditas’, meaning greening power. By this she meant the liveliness given by God in plants, animals and people.
67229.m: Hildegard spoke of the greening power of nature.

67230.q: Roughly how old was Hildegard of Bingen when she died?
67230.e: Hildegard was born in 1098 and died on 17 September 1179. So she lived to about 81, which was very old for the Middle Ages.
67230.m: Hildegard lived to a great age for her time.

67231.q: Which order did Thomas Aquinas join?
67231.e: Against his family's wishes, Thomas joined the young Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. This order placed great value on study and preaching.

67232.q: How did Thomas's family react when he wanted to become a begging friar?
a: They moved with him to Paris
67232.e: His noble family wanted him to become abbot of a rich monastery. So his brothers held him in a castle for more than a year.
67232.m: Thomas's family held him prisoner for a while.

67233.q: In which present-day country was Thomas Aquinas born?
67233.e: Thomas was born around 1225 at Roccasecca Castle near Aquino. The place lies between Rome and Naples.

67234.q: Shortly before his death, what did Thomas Aquinas compare everything he had written to?
67234.e: After a deep experience in prayer in 1273, Thomas stopped writing. He is said to have said that everything he had written seemed like straw compared to it.
67234.m: In the end Thomas compared his writings to straw.

67235.q: What nickname did fellow students give the quiet, sturdy Thomas?
67235.e: Because Thomas was quiet and big, fellow students called him the ‘dumb ox’. Albertus Magnus is said to have said that one day the whole world would hear this ox bellow.
67235.m: Thomas was mocked as the ‘dumb ox’.

67236.q: Which Greek philosopher did Thomas Aquinas rely on especially strongly?
67236.e: Thomas combined the teaching of Aristotle with the Christian faith. He wanted to show that faith and reason fit together.
67236.m: Thomas combined Aristotle with the faith.

67237.q: For which church feast did Thomas Aquinas write prayers and hymns at the pope's request?
67237.e: In 1264 Pope Urban IV introduced the feast of Corpus Christi for the whole Church. Thomas wrote texts for it such as the hymn ‘Pange lingua’.
67237.m: Thomas Aquinas wrote hymns for Corpus Christi.

67238.q: At which famous university did Thomas Aquinas teach as a professor?
67238.e: Thomas was a master of theology at the University of Paris. Later he also taught in Italy, for example in Naples.
67238.m: Thomas taught at the University of Paris.

67239.q: What did Thomas Aquinas want to show with his thinking?
a: That faith and reason fit together
That the Church does not need a pope
67239.e: Thomas thought through the faith with precise questions and logical arguments. This medieval way of thinking is called scholasticism.
67239.m: Thomas Aquinas combined faith and reason.

67240.q: What punishment did the Church impose on Jan Hus in 1410?
a: A ban on writing in Latin
67240.e: With excommunication, Hus was shut out of the community of the Church. In 1411 the antipope John XXIII excommunicated him again.

67241.q: At which council was Jan Hus condemned?
67241.e: The Council of Constance on Lake Constance met from 1414 to 1418. It condemned Hus as a heretic, right on the border with today's Switzerland near Kreuzlingen.
67241.m: Jan Hus was condemned in Constance.

67242.q: What happened to Jan Hus's ashes after he was burnt?
a: They were scattered in the Rhine
They were kept in a church
67242.e: The executioners scattered the ashes in the Rhine. That way there would be no grave for his followers to honour.
67242.m: Jan Hus's ashes were scattered in the Rhine.

67243.q: Which ordination did Jan Hus receive in 1400?
67243.e: Hus was ordained a priest in 1400. After that he worked as a pastor and preacher.
67243.m: Jan Hus became a priest in 1400.

67244.q: Which innovation in Czech writing is credited to Jan Hus?
67244.e: Hus is thought to be the author of a work that suggested marks such as accents and dots above letters. Today's special Czech characters developed from this, although it is not completely certain that he wrote it.
67244.m: The Czech marks above letters probably go back to Hus.

67245.q: In which city is the great Jan Hus Memorial?
67245.e: The memorial stands in the Old Town Square in Prague. It was unveiled in 1915 for the 500th anniversary of Hus's death.
67245.m: The great Hus Memorial is in Prague.

67246.q: What has the anniversary of Jan Hus's death been in the Czech lands since 1925?
67246.e: Czechoslovakia declared 6 July a public holiday in 1925. It is also a holiday in today's Czech Republic.
67246.m: Jan Hus Day is a public holiday in the Czech Republic.

67247.q: What happened to Jan Hus in Constance in 1415?
a: He was burnt as a heretic
67247.e: The Council of Constance condemned Hus as a heretic. He was burnt on 6 July 1415. Today the Hus Stone recalls this.
67247.m: Jan Hus was burnt in Constance in 1415.

67248.q: Which order did Ignatius of Loyola found?
67248.e: Ignatius founded the Society of Jesus with companions. Pope Paul III approved the order in 1540.

67249.q: Which region of Spain did Ignatius of Loyola come from?
67249.e: Ignatius was born in 1491 at Loyola Castle in the Basque Country. He came from a noble family.

67250.q: What happened to Ignatius in 1521 during the defence of Pamplona?
a: He became bishop of the city
67250.e: A cannonball badly wounded his leg. During his long recovery he read stories of the saints and turned to God.
67250.m: A war wound led Ignatius to faith.

67252.q: Which abbreviation comes after the names of Jesuits?
67252.e: SJ stands for Societas Jesu, Latin for Society of Jesus. OSB, for example, is the abbreviation of the Benedictines.

67253.q: Which office did Ignatius take on in the newly founded Jesuit order?
67253.e: His companions elected Ignatius as the first Superior General in 1541. He led the order until his death in Rome in 1556.
67253.m: Ignatius was the first Superior General of the Jesuits.

67254.q: Which country did Ignatius of Loyola come from?
67254.e: Ignatius was born in 1491 in the Basque Country in northern Spain. Loyola is the name of his family's castle.

67255.q: What is the Latin motto of the Jesuits, AMDG for short?
a: For the greater glory of God
67255.e: AMDG stands for ‘Ad maiorem Dei gloriam’, meaning ‘For the greater glory of God’. Everything they do should honour God.
67255.m: Jesuits want to do everything for the greater glory of God.

67256.q: In which country did Teresa of Ávila live?
67256.e: Teresa was born in 1515 in Ávila in Castile. She lived and worked in Spain.

67257.q: How did Teresa of Ávila live for most of her life?
a: As a nun in a convent
As a farmer on a farm
67257.e: Teresa entered a Carmelite convent in Ávila when she was young. Later she founded many new convents herself.
67257.m: Teresa of Ávila was a nun.

67258.q: Why are the sisters of Teresa's reformed order called ‘Discalced’, meaning shoeless?
a: They wore simple sandals instead of shoes
They were never allowed to leave the convent
67258.e: The sisters of the reform lived very simply. Instead of shoes they wore plain sandals, which is why they are called Discalced Carmelites.
67258.m: Teresa's sisters wore sandals instead of shoes.

67259.q: What is Teresa of Ávila still known for today?
67259.e: Teresa wrote several books about prayer and the path to God. In ‘The Interior Castle’ she compares the soul to a castle.
67259.m: Teresa of Ávila wrote famous books about prayer.

67260.q: In 1970 Teresa of Ávila became the first woman ‘Doctor of the Church’. What does that mean?
a: Her writings count as important teaching for the whole Church
She taught children in a school
67260.e: Pope Paul VI made Teresa a Doctor of the Church in 1970. In this way the Church says that her writings are especially valuable for all believers.
67260.m: Teresa of Ávila was the first woman Doctor of the Church.

67261.q: Teresa of Ávila and her helper John of the Cross are regarded as great mystics. What is a mystic?
a: A person who wants to be very close to God in prayer
A scientist who watches the stars
A knight who defends a castle
67261.e: Mystics seek a deep encounter with God in silent prayer. John of the Cross also helped Teresa reform her order.
67261.m: Mystics seek closeness to God in prayer.

67262.q: In which language did Teresa of Ávila write her well-known prayer ‘Nada te turbe’?
67262.e: ‘Nada te turbe’ is Spanish and means ‘Let nothing disturb you’. The Taizé Community made a well-known song out of it.
67262.m: ‘Nada te turbe’ is a Spanish prayer by Teresa of Ávila.

67263.q: What was special about the night in October 1582 when Teresa died?
67263.e: Teresa died on the night that Spain introduced the Gregorian calendar. 4 October was followed directly by 15 October.
67263.m: Teresa died on the night of the calendar reform.

67264.q: What was special about Dietrich Bonhoeffer's birth?
a: He was born on a ship
67264.e: Dietrich and his twin sister Sabine were born in 1906. Sabine later had to flee from the Nazis to England.
67264.m: Dietrich Bonhoeffer had a twin sister.

67265.q: In which city did Dietrich Bonhoeffer grow up and study?
67265.e: The family moved to Berlin, where his father was a professor. Dietrich studied and later taught at the University of Berlin.

67266.q: Who did Bonhoeffer train from 1935 on behalf of the Confessing Church?
67266.e: At the seminary in Finkenwalde, Bonhoeffer trained young pastors. In 1937 the Gestapo had the seminary closed.

67267.q: Why was Dietrich Bonhoeffer arrested in 1943?
a: Because of his resistance to the Nazis
Because he wanted to travel abroad
67267.e: Bonhoeffer was in contact with men who wanted to overthrow Hitler. The Gestapo arrested him on 5 April 1943.
67267.m: Bonhoeffer went to prison because of his resistance.

67268.q: How did Bonhoeffer live together with the young pastors at the seminary?
a: Like a household with prayer and work
Each alone in his own flat
67268.e: Bonhoeffer and the trainee pastors prayed, ate and worked together. In 1939 he wrote the book ‘Life Together’ about it.
67268.m: Bonhoeffer lived with his students as a household community.

67269.q: How did Bonhoeffer keep in touch with his fiancée and his family from prison?
67269.e: Bonhoeffer was engaged to Maria von Wedemeyer. They wrote each other many letters while he was in prison, but they were never able to marry.
67269.m: Bonhoeffer wrote many letters from prison.

67270.q: What did Bonhoeffer call on the churches of the world to work for at a conference in 1934?
67270.e: On the island of Fanø in Denmark, Bonhoeffer gave a famous speech for peace. Even then he warned of a new war.
67270.m: Bonhoeffer called on the churches to work for peace.

67271.q: Why is there a statue of Bonhoeffer on Westminster Abbey in London?
a: He is honoured as a martyr of the 20th century
67271.e: Since 1998, ten statues of 20th-century martyrs have stood above the west door. One of them shows Dietrich Bonhoeffer.
67271.m: Bonhoeffer is honoured as a martyr.

67272.q: When did Mother Teresa get the name Teresa?
a: When she won the Nobel Peace Prize
When she was made a saint
67272.e: Mother Teresa's real name was Agnes. She chose the name Teresa when she became a nun.
67272.m: Mother Teresa got her name in the convent.

67273.q: Who did Mother Teresa name herself after when choosing her religious name?
67273.e: She chose her name after the French saint Thérèse of Lisieux. Thérèse is the patron saint of missionaries.
67273.m: Mother Teresa named herself after a saint.

67274.q: Where did Mother Teresa feel her ‘call within a call’ to serve the poor in September 1946?
67274.e: On 10 September 1946 she travelled by train to Darjeeling. There she felt the call to leave the convent and live among the poorest of the poor.
67274.m: On a train journey Mother Teresa felt her call to the poor.

67275.q: Which citizenship did Mother Teresa take on as a nun in Calcutta?
67275.e: Mother Teresa became an Indian citizen. She wanted to belong completely to the people she served.

67276.q: What honour did India give Mother Teresa after her death in 1997?
67276.e: India honoured Mother Teresa with a state funeral, which is otherwise mainly given to politicians. People of all religions mourned her.
67276.m: Mother Teresa was given a state funeral in India.

67277.q: In the Catholic Church, what is the step before being declared a saint, which Mother Teresa went through in 2003?
67277.e: Before someone is declared a saint, they are beatified. Mother Teresa was beatified in 2003 and declared a saint in 2016.
67277.m: Beatification comes before being declared a saint.

67278.q: What was Mother Teresa already before she founded her own order?
67278.e: At 18 she joined the Loreto Sisters and taught at their school in Calcutta. Only in 1950 did she found her own order.
67278.m: Mother Teresa was a nun first.

67279.q: What did Mother Teresa open in Calcutta in 1952?
67279.e: In the Nirmal Hriday home, dying people from the streets could spend their last days with dignity. The sisters cared for them whatever their religion.
67279.m: Mother Teresa gave the dying a home.

67281.q: In which city in Alabama did Martin Luther King become pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in 1954?
67281.e: King took over the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery in 1954. A year later the famous bus boycott began there.
67281.m: King was a pastor in Montgomery.

67282.q: Why was Martin Luther King also called ‘Dr King’?
a: He had a doctorate in theology
It was his nickname from school
67282.e: King wrote a doctoral thesis in theology in 1955. From then on he was also called ‘Dr King’.
67282.m: Martin Luther King had a doctorate in theology.

67283.q: Who mainly helped Martin Luther King organise the non-violent protests?
67283.e: In 1957 King founded an association with other pastors from the southern states. The church congregations organised marches and boycotts against racial segregation.
67283.m: Churches and pastors helped King with his protests.

67284.q: What did Martin Luther King call for in his sermons, even towards his opponents?
67284.e: King preached that you should love even your enemies, as Jesus taught. His sermons appeared in 1963 in the book ‘Strength to Love’.
67284.m: King preached love instead of hate.

67285.q: In which city did Martin Luther King preach in both the western and the eastern part in 1964, although a wall divided the city?
67285.e: In September 1964 King spoke in West Berlin and on the same day also preached in St Mary's Church in East Berlin. Many people came to hear him.
67285.m: In 1964 King preached in both parts of Berlin.

67286.q: Which person from the Bible did King recall in his last speech, when he said he had seen the promised land?
67286.e: On the evening before his death, King said he had been to the mountaintop and seen the promised land. Moses also saw the promised land from a mountain but did not enter it.
67286.m: King's last speech recalled Moses on the mountain.

67287.q: According to a Bible verse that King liked to quote, what should roll down like waters?
67287.e: King often quoted the prophet Amos: let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
67287.m: King wanted justice that rolls down like water.

67288.q: What was Pope Francis especially known for?
67288.e: Francis did without the large papal apartment and lived in the Vatican guest house Santa Marta. He worked especially for poor people.

67289.q: In which year was Jorge Mario Bergoglio elected pope?
67289.e: On 13 March 2013 the cardinals elected Bergoglio as pope. He was the first pope from the Americas.

67290.q: Which country did Pope Francis come from?
67290.e: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born in Buenos Aires in 1936. He was archbishop of that city before he became pope.

67291.q: Which saint did Pope Francis name himself after?
67291.e: Bergoglio chose the name after Francis of Assisi, who lived in poverty and cared for the poor and for creation. No pope before him had been called Francis.
67291.m: Pope Francis named himself after Francis of Assisi.

67292.q: What topic does Pope Francis's encyclical ‘Laudato si'’ from 2015 deal with?
67292.e: In ‘Laudato si'’ Francis calls on people to protect the earth as our common home. The title comes from the Canticle of the Sun by Francis of Assisi.
67292.m: ‘Laudato si'’ is about protecting the earth.

67293.q: Which pope was in office directly before Francis and resigned of his own free will?
67293.e: Benedict XVI resigned in February 2013 because of his age. That was a very rare step in Church history.
67293.m: Before Francis, Benedict XVI was pope.

67294.q: In which year did Pope Francis die?
67294.e: Pope Francis died on 21 April 2025, Easter Monday. His successor, Pope Leo XIV, was elected in May 2025.

67295.q: Which Swiss city did Pope Francis visit in 2018 for the 70th anniversary of the World Council of Churches?
67295.e: On 21 June 2018 Francis travelled to Geneva, where the World Council of Churches is based. There he also celebrated Mass in front of thousands of believers.

67296.q: Which Geneva society did Henri Dunant join at 18 to help the poor and prisoners?
67296.e: Dunant became a member of the ‘Société d'Aumônes’, a society for giving alms. In his free time he visited prisoners and helped poor people.
67296.m: Even as a young man Dunant helped the poor and prisoners.

67297.q: Which Christian youth organisation did Henri Dunant help to set up in Geneva?
67297.e: In 1852 Dunant co-founded a group of the Young Men's Christian Association in Geneva and was its secretary. He also worked for a worldwide link between these associations.
67297.m: Henri Dunant helped set up the YMCA.

67298.q: Which denomination did Henri Dunant belong to?
67298.e: Dunant grew up in a devout Calvinist family in Geneva. His faith drove him to help those who were suffering.
67298.m: Henri Dunant was a Reformed Christian.

67299.q: What drove Henri Dunant to help the poor and the wounded?
67299.e: Dunant grew up in a devout Geneva family and was shaped by a Protestant revival movement. For him, love of your neighbour was part of faith.
67299.m: Dunant's faith drove him to help.

67300.q: Which cry of the women helpers in Castiglione became famous through Henri Dunant?
67300.e: ‘Tutti fratelli’ means ‘We are all brothers’. The women cared for wounded soldiers, no matter which country they came from.
67300.m: ‘Tutti fratelli’ means that all people are brothers.

67301.q: Why did Henri Dunant travel to northern Italy in 1859?
a: To go on a seaside holiday
67301.e: Dunant wanted help for his business in North Africa from the French Emperor Napoleon III. That is how he came by chance to the battlefield of Solferino.
67301.m: Dunant came to Solferino because of his business.

67302.q: How did Henri Dunant describe himself in a letter in his old age?
a: As a disciple of Christ as in the first century
As a loyal servant of the pope
As a preacher of the Geneva church
As a monk without a monastery
67302.e: Dunant wrote: ‘I am a disciple of Christ as in the first century, and nothing more.’ His faith in Christ stayed important to him to the end.
67302.m: Dunant saw himself as a simple disciple of Christ.

67303.q: What did Henri Dunant turn away from in the last years of his life?
67303.e: In his old age Dunant turned away from Calvinism and from all churches as organisations. But he remained a believing Christian.
67303.m: In old age Dunant kept his distance from the churches.

67304.q: In which empire was the Blue Mosque built?
67304.e: The mosque was built from 1609 to 1616 under Sultan Ahmed I. Istanbul was then the capital of the Ottoman Empire.
67304.m: The Blue Mosque is an Ottoman building.

67305.q: Whose pupil was the architect of the Blue Mosque?
67305.e: The architect Mehmed Ağa had learned from the great Ottoman architect Mimar Sinan. He took on many of his teacher's ideas.
67305.m: The architect of the Blue Mosque was a pupil of Mimar Sinan.

67306.q: Why is it bright inside the Blue Mosque during the day?
a: Light comes in through many windows
The roof is made of glass
67306.e: Daylight comes into the prayer hall through about 260 windows. Today's coloured glass windows are copies of the old ones.
67306.m: Many windows make the Blue Mosque bright inside.

67307.q: What supports the large main dome of the Blue Mosque?
67307.e: The main dome is about 43 metres high. Several half-domes around it carry and support it.
67307.m: Half-domes support the main dome of the Blue Mosque.

67308.q: Where is Sultan Ahmed I buried?
a: In a tomb building next to the Blue Mosque
In the Taj Mahal in Agra
67308.e: Sultan Ahmed I rests in a türbe, a tomb building right next to his mosque. Members of his family, including later sultans, also lie there.
67308.m: Sultan Ahmed I is buried in a tomb building next to his mosque.

67309.q: What was a pope's visit to the Blue Mosque in 2006 meant to show?
a: That Christians and Muslims want to talk to each other
That the mosque would become a church
That the pope would become a Muslim
That the mosque would be closed
67309.e: Pope Benedict XVI visited the mosque in November 2006. It was a sign of dialogue between the religions.
67309.m: A papal visit in 2006 was a sign of dialogue between religions.

67310.q: Roughly how many handmade tiles decorate the inside of the Blue Mosque?
67310.e: More than 20,000 ceramic tiles with flowers and patterns were used inside. They gave the mosque its well-known nickname.
67310.m: More than 20,000 tiles decorate the Blue Mosque.

67311.q: What is the Blue Mosque today?
a: A mosque where people still pray
Only a museum with no prayers
67311.e: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque is still used for prayers today. Tourists may visit it outside prayer times.
67311.m: Muslims still pray in the Blue Mosque today.

67312.q: Who had the magnificent palaces of the Alhambra built?
67312.e: The Nasrids ruled the Emirate of Granada from the 13th century until 1492. The magnificent palaces were built during this time.
67312.m: Muslim rulers built the palaces of the Alhambra.

67313.q: In which Spanish city is the Alhambra?
67313.e: The Alhambra stands on a hill above Granada in Andalusia. Until 1492 it was the seat of the Muslim rulers.

67315.q: Which ruler had a Renaissance-style palace built in the Alhambra?
67315.e: Charles V ordered the palace in 1527. It was never fully finished and today houses museums.
67315.m: In the middle of the Alhambra stands a Renaissance palace of Charles V.

67316.q: Which country did the writer Washington Irving come from, who made the Alhambra famous with his stories?
67316.e: The American Washington Irving lived in the Alhambra for a few months in 1829. His “Tales of the Alhambra” attracted many travellers to Granada.
67316.m: Washington Irving made the Alhambra famous with his stories.

67317.q: What was the Alcazaba, the oldest part of the Alhambra, used for?
67317.e: The Alcazaba is the military part with towers and walls. From there soldiers kept watch over the city.
67317.m: The Alcazaba is the fortress of the Alhambra.

67318.q: Which Dutch artist was inspired by the tile patterns of the Alhambra?
67318.e: M. C. Escher copied the tile patterns in the Alhambra. After that he created his famous pictures of figures that fit together without gaps.
67318.m: The patterns of the Alhambra inspired the artist M. C. Escher.

67319.q: What was the name of the woman for whom the Taj Mahal was built as a tomb?
67319.e: Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built for his favourite wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Her name means something like “the chosen one of the palace”.
67319.m: The Taj Mahal is the tomb of Mumtaz Mahal.

67320.q: In which century was the Taj Mahal built?
67320.e: Building began in 1632, shortly after the death of Mumtaz Mahal. The whole site was only finished after many years.
67320.m: The Taj Mahal was built in the 17th century.

67321.q: Roughly how many craftsmen worked on the Taj Mahal?
67321.e: More than 20,000 craftsmen from India and other countries worked on the Taj Mahal. About 1,000 elephants helped to transport the building materials.
67321.m: Over 20,000 craftsmen built the Taj Mahal.

67322.q: Why do the four minarets of the Taj Mahal lean slightly outwards?
a: So that they would not fall onto the tomb in an earthquake
Because the ground was too soft
67322.e: The minarets lean slightly on purpose. If they collapsed, they would fall away from the main building.
67322.m: The minarets of the Taj Mahal lean outwards to protect the tomb.

67323.q: What are the coloured flower patterns in the white marble of the Taj Mahal made with?
67323.e: Craftsmen cut semi-precious stones precisely and set them into the marble. This created flowers and bands of writing that never fade.
67323.m: The patterns on the Taj Mahal are made of inlaid semi-precious stones.

a: In the Taj Mahal next to his wife
67324.e: Shah Jahan's sarcophagus stands next to his wife's. Because it was added later, it is the only element that is not placed symmetrically.
67324.m: Shah Jahan rests in the Taj Mahal next to Mumtaz Mahal.

67325.q: How is the garden in front of the Taj Mahal laid out?
a: In four equal parts with water channels
As a rock garden without plants
67325.e: The garden is a charbagh, a Persian garden in four parts. In the middle there is a long pool in which the tomb is reflected.
67325.m: The garden of the Taj Mahal is divided into four parts.

67326.q: Which famous list is the Taj Mahal on because it is valuable for all of humanity?
67326.e: UNESCO has added the Taj Mahal to the World Heritage List. Such places are to be preserved for all people.
67326.m: The Taj Mahal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

67327.q: Why is the Arabic script Naskh the one most often used for books today?
a: Because it is easy to read
Because it is the oldest script
Because it runs from left to right
67327.e: Naskh is clear and easy to read. That is why it is used most for books and the printed Quran.
67327.m: Naskh is the most common Arabic book script.

67328.q: Where do you often see Arabic calligraphy as large, sweeping bands of writing?
a: On the walls and domes of mosques
67328.e: Grand scripts such as Thuluth decorate the walls and domes of many mosques. They often show verses from the Quran.
67328.m: Mosques are often decorated with large bands of writing.

67329.q: Which language apart from Arabic is also written with Arabic letters?
67329.e: Persian is written with Arabic letters. The elegant, hanging script style Nastaliq also developed in Persia.
67329.m: Persian is also written with Arabic letters.

67330.q: Why did the Ottomans write their official documents in a very dense, ornate script?
a: So that they were beautiful and hard to forge
So that they could be read faster
Because children were meant to write them
67330.e: The Diwani script developed in the Ottoman chancery, the Divan. The dense script was beautiful and hard to forge.
67330.m: The Ottomans wrote their official documents in the Diwani script.

67331.q: Why is the Prophet Muhammad often described in Islamic art with words instead of a picture?
a: Because many Muslims do not show him in pictures
Because there were no colours at the time
67331.e: Many Muslims do not show Muhammad in pictures. A panel of writing, the hilye, therefore describes his appearance and character in words.
67331.m: A hilye describes Muhammad with artistic writing instead of a picture.

67332.q: North-west Africa is called the Maghreb in Arabic. What does this word mean?
67332.e: Maghreb means “west”, the land where the sun sets. The Maghribi script style also comes from there.

67334.q: What is typical of the everyday Arabic script Ruq'a?
a: It can be written quickly by hand
It is only used for the Quran
It runs from left to right
67334.e: Ruq'a has short, simple shapes and can be written quickly. Many people in Arab countries use it for handwriting.
67334.m: Ruq'a is a fast everyday script.

67335.q: In which direction is Arabic script written?
67335.e: Arabic is written from right to left. That is why, from our point of view, an Arabic book begins “at the back”.
67335.m: Arabic is written from right to left.

67336.q: The word “arabesque” originally comes from which language?
67336.e: The word comes from the Italian “arabesco”, which means “Arabic”. Europeans used it for the decoration they knew from Islamic art.

67337.q: What is special about the pattern of an arabesque?
67337.e: An arabesque has no fixed beginning and no end. Many see this as a sign of God's infinity.
67337.m: An arabesque can be continued without end.

67338.q: For which instrument did Robert Schumann write his piece “Arabeske” in 1839?
67338.e: Robert Schumann composed the “Arabeske”, Op. 18, for piano. Like the ornament, the music is playful and intertwined.
67338.m: Robert Schumann wrote a piano piece called “Arabeske”.

67339.q: Claude Debussy wrote the well-known “Deux Arabesques”. What was Debussy's job?
67339.e: Claude Debussy was a French composer. His two arabesques for piano are among his best-known pieces.
67339.m: Claude Debussy composed two arabesques for piano.

67340.q: What is an arabesque in ballet?
a: A pose on one leg with the other leg stretched out behind
67340.e: In an arabesque the dancer stands on one leg and stretches the other far out behind. The long line recalls the sweeping ornament.
67340.m: In ballet, the arabesque is a pose on one leg.

67341.q: What are the colourful zellige patterns in Morocco made of?
67341.e: Zellige are mosaics made of hand-cut clay tiles. In Morocco they decorate fountains, walls and floors.

67342.e: Arabesques are mainly made of curving plant shapes. Tendrils, leaves and flowers seem to grow into each other endlessly.
67342.m: Arabesques are made of plant shapes.

67343.q: What shapes are many geometric patterns in Islamic art made of?
67343.e: Such patterns are called girih, which means “knot” in Persian. Crossing lines form stars and polygons.
67343.m: Girih patterns are made of stars and polygons.

67344.q: What does the abbreviation “AH” after an Islamic year mean?
a: In the year of the Hijra
67344.e: The Islamic calendar counts the years from Muhammad's emigration to Medina. That is why you write, for example, “1448 AH”.
67344.m: The abbreviation “AH” means “in the year of the Hijra”.

67345.q: What do many Muslims celebrate in the month of Rabi al-Awwal?
67345.e: The festival is called Mawlid an-Nabi and for many Sunnis falls on 12 Rabi al-Awwal. Shias often celebrate it a few days later.
67345.m: In the month of Rabi al-Awwal many Muslims celebrate Muhammad's birthday.

67346.q: In which month of our calendar did the Islamic year 1448 begin?
67346.e: The Islamic New Year 1448 fell in mid-June 2026. Because the lunar year is shorter, the year 1449 begins about eleven days earlier, still in June 2027.
67346.m: The Islamic year 1448 began in June 2026.

67347.q: Traditionally, how do you recognise the beginning of a new Islamic month?
a: By the first thin crescent moon
67347.e: The month begins when the first crescent moon, the hilal, can be seen after the new moon. Today some countries also calculate the start in advance.
67347.m: An Islamic month begins with the first crescent moon.

67348.q: On which day of the month of Muharram is the day of remembrance Ashura?
67348.e: Ashura comes from the Arabic word for ten. On this day Shias especially remember the death of Husayn at Karbala.
67348.m: Ashura is on the tenth day of Muharram.

67349.q: A lunar month lasts about 29.5 days. How many days do 12 such months have together?
67349.e: 12 times 29.5 days makes 354 days. That is about 11 days fewer than a solar year of 365 days.
67349.m: Twelve lunar months last about 354 days together.

67350.q: Which country officially uses an Islamic solar calendar whose year begins at the start of spring?
67350.e: Iran also counts the years from the Hijra, but by the sun. New Year is the Nowruz festival at the beginning of spring.
67350.m: Iran has an Islamic solar calendar with New Year in spring.

67351.q: How many days can a month in the Islamic calendar have?
67351.e: About 29.5 days pass from one crescent moon to the next. That is why a month has either 29 or 30 days.
67351.m: An Islamic month has 29 or 30 days.

67352.q: Which animal is basically forbidden by Islamic food rules?
67352.e: The Quran clearly forbids pork. Meat from cattle, sheep and goats is allowed if it has been slaughtered correctly.

67353.q: Why do many Muslims check the ingredients of jelly sweets?
a: Because gelatine often comes from pigs
67353.e: Gelatine is often made from pig skin. But there are also jelly sweets made with beef gelatine or plant ingredients.
67353.m: Gelatine in sweets often comes from pigs.

67354.q: What does a halal certificate confirm?
a: That a product is allowed by Islamic rules
That a product comes from Switzerland
That a product is especially cheap
67354.e: An inspection body checks the ingredients and how the product is made. If it meets the rules, it may carry a halal mark.
67354.m: A halal certificate confirms that a product is allowed.

67355.q: What has been banned in Switzerland since a popular vote in 1893?
67355.e: In 1893 the people approved the first federal popular initiative, the ban on ritual slaughter. Today the Animal Welfare Act says that mammals must be stunned before slaughter.
67355.m: In Switzerland mammals must be stunned before slaughter.

67356.q: So where do Muslims in Switzerland often get ritually slaughtered meat from?
67356.e: Importing meat from religious slaughter is allowed. This is how Muslims and Jews in Switzerland get meat according to their rules.
67356.m: Ritually slaughtered meat may be imported into Switzerland.

67357.q: In which Asian country does a state authority issue a halal mark that is known worldwide?
67357.e: In Malaysia the state authority JAKIM issues the halal mark. Its certificate is recognised in many countries.
67357.m: In Malaysia a state authority checks whether products are halal.

67358.q: What do many Muslims do if it is unclear whether a food is halal?
a: They prefer to go without it.
They only eat it on Fridays.
They simply cook it for longer.
67358.e: Doubtful foods are called mashbooh. Many Muslims avoid them until it is clear what they are made of.
67358.m: With doubtful foods, many Muslims prefer to go without.

67359.q: Apart from food, which products can also have halal certificates?
67359.e: Creams, lipsticks or capsules can also contain substances from pigs or alcohol. That is why some companies have them certified.
67359.m: Cosmetics and medicines can also be certified halal.

67360.q: What is forbidden in Islamic banking?
67360.e: The Quran forbids riba, which is usually understood as interest. Islamic banks therefore earn their money in other ways.
67360.m: Islamic banks do not charge interest.

67361.q: What is the Arabic word for the forbidden interest?
67361.e: Riba literally means “increase”. It refers to a fixed, agreed profit from money that is lent.
67361.m: The forbidden interest is called riba.

a: The bank buys goods and sells them on at a mark-up
The bank charges interest every month
67362.e: For example, the bank buys a car and sells it to the customer at a higher, fixed price. The customer pays it off in instalments, without interest.
67362.m: With murabaha the bank earns from a price mark-up.

67363.q: Where does the return on Islamic bonds, called sukuk, come from?
a: From rents or profits of a real asset
67363.e: Anyone who buys sukuk gets a share in an asset such as a building. The return comes from rents or profits instead of interest.
67363.m: Sukuk are Islamic bonds without interest.

67364.q: How does the Islamic insurance takaful work?
a: Members pay into a shared pot and help each other
Everyone only pays when they are ill
67364.e: With takaful, members pay into a shared pot. From it they help each other when damage or loss happens.
67364.m: Takaful is insurance according to Islamic rules.

67365.q: Which businesses are Islamic banks not allowed to invest in?
67365.e: Businesses involving alcohol, pork or gambling are considered haram. A board of scholars checks the bank's investments.
67365.m: Islamic banks do not invest in gambling and alcohol.

67366.q: What does mudaraba mean in Islamic banking?
a: One person gives money, the other does the work, and they share the profit
67366.e: In mudaraba, one person provides the capital and the other their knowledge and work. Profits are shared according to an agreed ratio.
67366.m: In mudaraba, the investor and the entrepreneur share the profit.

67367.q: In which country does the Islamic Development Bank have its headquarters?
